extracted.subtask_description: An illustrated, conversational natural-history textbook excerpt that explains insect anatomy, life cycles, behavior, and ecology for children using dialogue, examples, and simple demonstrations. Emphasizes observable detail, labelled parts, and engaging storytelling to teach basic entomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational/dialogic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the child reader directly through questions and short dialogues (e.g., 'Children, here is a cockroach.' 'What is that, May?'), using a friendly, informal narrator-child interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ Q&A and brief exchanges to anticipate curiosity, model inquiry, and keep tone engaging and accessible. Use short sentences, rhetorical questions, and direct prompts to maintain attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include illustrations and specimen displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide pictures or physical specimen views repeatedly throughout the text (numerous '[Illustration]' references, glass-topped box to view a specimen), so readers can see the organism being described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place illustrations at points where anatomy, behavior, or lifecycle is discussed; use close-ups for small structures and labelled diagrams for parts. Recommend safe specimen display methods (e.g., glass-top box) for observation without handling risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe life cycle and metamorphosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain where eggs are laid, larval form and feeding, moulting, seasonal hiding, and emergence into the adult (e.g., 'It lays its eggs in the water... larvæ... moults several times... emerges ... as a perfect winged insect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover each major stage (egg, larva/nymph, moulting, adult), timing (seasonality), feeding at each stage, and notable behaviors (e.g., hiding in winter). Use simple chronological narrative and concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe habitat, diet, and ecological interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: State where the insect lives, what it eats, its predators, and how it interacts with other organisms and humans (e.g., stone fly under stones and eaten by fish; cockroaches in pantries; mantis preying on insects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include microhabitat details (under stones, in water, pantries), feeding preferences, risks (predation, being used as bait), and roles (pest, predator, prey) to situate the insect ecologically and practically for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce anatomical terminology with labels and mnemonics
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the proper names of body parts and segments (e.g., coxa, trochanter, femur, tibia, tarsus) and support memorization with labels and a jingle: 'Coxa first, and then trochanter...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine labelled diagrams with verbal mnemonics, stepwise labelling (I–V), and brief definitions of each term. Encourage repetition and drawing to reinforce terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies and familiar-object demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain unfamiliar structures or motions by comparison to everyday objects or simple physical demonstrations (e.g., antennae like threads, wing covers like a roof, ball-and-socket joint demonstrated by fitting a fist into a palm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select analogies rooted in children's experience (sticks, roofs, fists). When possible, include a short hands-on demonstration readers can do to visualize the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage hands-on observation and drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt readers to observe specimens with magnifying glasses, to draw what they see, and to perform small observation activities (e.g., 'Let us draw a picture of the long hind leg', 'look at the grasshopper's foot through the magnifying glass').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit activity prompts, step-by-step drawing suggestions, and simple tools (magnifying glass, tumbler, box). Emphasize patience and repeated attempts ('Any child can learn to draw who will keep trying').

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain structure–function relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Link anatomical features to their functions in plain cause–effect terms (e.g., spines prevent slipping, pulvillus sticky hairs allow walking on glass, wing covers protect inner wings and lock open during flight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a structure is named, add a short explanation of what it does and why it matters to the insect's survival or behavior. Use simple experiments or observations to demonstrate function when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note species variation, sexual dimorphism, and geographic differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out differences among species, male/female variation (e.g., male cockroach with wings, female with rudimentary wings), and distributional differences (tropical origin, spread via ships, abundance North vs South).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasting examples to show diversity. Mention cultural/local names and variants (croton bug, water bugs) and caution that forms and habits can vary by region and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use storytelling, humor, and mild personification to engage
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply playful names and short stories, mild anthropomorphism and humorous asides (e.g., calling insects 'rascals', 'poor old cockroaches', mantis nicknames like 'mule-killer') to maintain interest while conveying facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance entertainment and accuracy: use personification to engage but follow with factual correction. Avoid misleading attributions of human motives; keep personification light and educational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give practical handling and safety advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer simple cautions and safe-handling recommendations woven into the narrative (e.g., keep specimen in a box with glass top, 'Do not kill needlessly', be careful because cockroaches give off an ill-smelling liquid, avoid unnecessary touching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit steps for safe observation (use containers, observe at night from a distance, avoid direct handling), and ethical notes about respecting living creatures unless necessary for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incremental organization from simple to complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure explanations by starting with simple, observable facts (appearance, where it lives), then moving to anatomy, function, behaviors, and broader ecological or cultural notes (e.g., begin with 'This is a cockroach' then proceed to legs, antennæ, reproductive cases, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence material so each new fact builds on prior observations; use repeated references back to earlier points (illustrations, labelled parts) to reinforce learning and avoid overwhelming the reader.
